item.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
item.description: arXiv:2610.33122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.
item.dc:creator: Bartosz Ziollko, Adam Niedzialkowski, Bartosz Szyma

item.title: Cutting Corners or Saving Lives? The Evolutionary Stability of Ethics in Pharma Medicine
item.description: arXiv:2610.33819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The pharmaceutical industry operates at the intersection of financial incentives, state oversight, and public scrutiny. We model corporate compliance with a three-population replicator system of ethical firms, active regulators, and active public scrutiny, whose payoffs are motivated by a prisoner's dilemma of first-mover advantage, an inspection game between firms and the FDA, and a volunteer's dilemma in early-stage research. The eight payoff constants are fitted by bounded L-BFGS-B optimization to composite indices for 2010--2024, and a fully sourced dataset of fifteen heavily penalized firms links the model's strategy types to R&D intensity and penalties. The calibrated system has no interior fixed point: an exact identity shows that public scrutiny decays at a rate set by the difference between the regulators' and the public's cost-to-benefit ratios. Without public scrutiny the firm--regulator dynamics are conformally Hamiltonian, so the two populations cycle neutrally around a center, and Lyapunov exponents give no evidence of chaos. Bureaucratic friction $k$, which enters compliance costs as $k^3$, organizes two thresholds: above $k^*\approx0.75$ regulators saturate and compliance rests on public scrutiny, and above $k^{**}\approx0.81$ compliance collapses. The empirical friction index crosses both between 2016 and 2020, as the compliance index falls from $0.85$ to $0.60$. Relative to revenue, penalties are highest for the firms with the lowest R&D intensity. Ethical compliance is therefore an oscillating rather than a permanent state, persisting only while friction stays below the combined incentive of subsidies, fines, and public penalties.
item.dc:creator: Alanna Polyak, Thomas Zdyrski

item.title: Interplay Between Network Heterogeneity and Activation Thresholds in Global Cascades
item.description: arXiv:2610.33927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The onset of global cascades in complex networks depends on both the distribution of activation thresholds and the underlying network topology. Here we investigate how these two sources of heterogeneity interact within the Watts threshold model, using beta-distributed activation thresholds and beta-binomial degree distributions to systematically vary their respective properties. Analyzing the onset of cascades from infinitesimal seeds, we identify two distinct boundaries governing the large-connectivity behavior of vulnerable branching. The first separates regimes in which increasing connectivity enhances or suppresses propagation, depending on the abundance of individuals with low activation thresholds. The second distinguishes two mechanisms of suppression: one controlled by the scarcity of low-threshold individuals and the other by the diminishing abundance of low-degree nodes as connectivity increases. At the boundary between these mechanisms, their competing contributions produce a logarithmic correction to the asymptotic scaling. Our results demonstrate how the interplay between network structure and individual activation thresholds determines the conditions for extensive propagation.
item.dc:creator: Aidan Meador-Woodruff, Gourab Ghoshal

item.title: Designing sustainability under Earth-system rate constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.34026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sustainability debates are monopolized by quantities: total energy use, material stocks, or recycling volumes. These metrics are informative, but they obscure a more fundamental constraint. On a materially closed but energetically open Earth, long-term viability is governed by rates: power density, areal power density, and the rate at which dispersed materials can be repurified under dif- fuse solar fluxes. We develop a physical framework that links technological metabolism, material dilution, and recycling limits through these rate con- straints. This perspective clarifies why many contemporary technologies remain viable only through stock drawdown and high-power buffering, and why green growth strategies often shift rather than resolve the underlying mismatch between industrial activity and Earth-system dynamics. We argue that long-term sustain- ability requires both quantitative reduction in aggregate industrial throughput toward rate-bounded regimes and the development of technologies qualitatively compatible with biospheric operating conditions.
item.dc:creator: Jos\'e Halloy, Petros Chatzimpiros, Fran\c{c}ois Graner, Thomas Gregor

item.title: Is the arXiv Apocalypse upon us? A break in preprint growth coincident with agentic AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.34449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As an experiment in agentic assisted analysis, we used an agentic AI model to analyse the effect of agentic AI on arXiv submissions; data acquisition, analysis and the first draft were carried out by the model under the author's direction. Monthly arXiv submissions have grown exponentially for three decades, at about $9\%$ per year. Fitting a piecewise log-linear trend with seasonal modulation to the full record, we find two post-pandemic breaks in growth rate. The first, in mid-2022, precedes ChatGPT and is carried by the expansion of AI research within computer science (CS); outside CS, growth from 2022 to 2025 remained at $8\%$ per year. The second, between December 2025 and February 2026, follows the release of models capable of extended autonomous work and is absent from the AI categories themselves. Since December 2025 submissions without a CS listing have run $17\%$ above trend, and in September 2026 total submissions reached a record $40\,363$. The excess is largest in mathematics, where submissions doubled within a year, and follows a gradient from formal and theoretical fields to experimental ones that is not ordered by surveyed rates of AI-tool adoption. In mathematics the increase is distributed across subfields and authors, two-thirds of it arising from a larger number of distinct authors rather than from a few prolific submitters. Across fields the clearest signature is a shift to single authorship: solo-authored papers rose by $70\%$ within a year in mathematics and condensed matter, and by $44\%$ in quantitative biology even as its total output fell, but not in experimental particle physics. The analysis is deliberately agnostic of LLM-detection methods: it uses only submission counts and metadata, with treatment timing fixed by calendar dates, and is therefore free of the outcome-triggered timing bias of author-level studies.
item.dc:creator: Carlo R. Contaldi

item.title: Competitive exploration in structured environments
item.description: arXiv:2610.34643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisms must constantly weigh exploiting the resources they know against exploring for better ones. When foragers compete, the best behavior for each forager also depends on what its competitors do. How does competition change the strategic balance between exploration and exploitation? Here we address this question in a minimal model: two $\epsilon$-greedy temporal-difference learners on a one-dimensional lattice, who start at a small reward at one end and are unaware of a larger reward at the other. For a lone forager, the optimal exploration rate increases monotonically with the value of the distant reward, and with its distance up to a critical distance. When two foragers share the lattice and split rewards, the choice of exploration rate becomes a game whose Nash equilibria have both foragers exploring, both staying, or one exploring while the other stays (anti-coordination). Under local best-response dynamics, pairs of foragers often converge on both exploring or both staying, even when anti-coordination would be socially optimal. This social dilemma arises for a wide range of parameters, and it persists even in a simplified model without explicit spatial structure. A minimal, naturalistic signal, in which one forager informs the other that it has found the distant reward, can remove many of the dilemmas in which both foragers explore, and can produce a Nash equilibrium whose collective payoff exceeds that of every outcome available without signaling.
item.dc:creator: James P. Wolfe, Joshua B. Plotkin

item.title: From AI-assisted to AI-native Industrial Control: Architecture, Agent Design, and Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2610.34773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The integration of AI and industrial control is rapidly transforming industrial automation. However, current approaches remain predominantly AI-assisted, where AI functions are incorporated as auxiliary components without fundamentally altering the underlying architecture of industrial control systems. Consequently, the potential of AI to enable higher levels of autonomy, adaptability, and continuous evolution remains underutilized. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control paradigm, which reconceptualizes industrial control systems by positioning AI as the intrinsic core rather than an external enhancement. The proposed paradigm is built upon an AI-native infrastructure and a collection of collaborative agentic AIs, each encapsulating a set of advanced skills. Among them, the industrial control agent plays a central role in orchestrating the system lifecycle. Through this paradigm, industrial control shifts from a closed, capability-oriented, human-driven, and passive engineering process to an open, task-oriented, intent-driven, and autonomous solution delivery mechanism. The paper further analyzes the key challenges of the AI-native paradigm from both AI and industrial control perspectives, including issues related to AI model reliability, formal verification, real-time assurance, and heterogeneous resource orchestration. Overall, this work outlines a forward-looking vision for industrial control in the AI era and identifies critical research directions toward autonomous, evolvable, and adaptive control systems in complex and dynamic industrial environments.
item.dc:creator: Lisi Liu, Bin Wang, Quan Tang, Chuan Pang, Feng Gao, Shengkai Liu

item.title: Multiplex relational event models of self-reported and perceived gossip
item.description: arXiv:2610.35162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gossiping is a complex social phenomenon that unfolds through multiple types of relations. Among other things, individuals may initiate gossiping about others as a result of believing themselves to be the target of gossip. These two processes, i.e., gossiping and gossip perception, form a dynamic multiplex network, where self-reported and perceived gossip ties coexist and can influence each other over time. We develop a multiplex relational event model to study the joint evolution of these two processes. The proposed model includes endogeneous covariates that capture the influence of events occurring within one layer, as well as events occurring on the other layer, on the rate of self-reported and perceived gossiping. We analyze survey data collected annually from 44 secondary schools in Hungary. We show how a multiplex relational event model, including linear, smooth and random effects, is able to describe the social mechanisms operating within and between self-reported and perceived gossiping and to capture how these two layers influence each other over time.
item.dc:creator: Veronica Poda, Veronica Vinciotti, Ernst C. Wit

item.title: Formation of international environmental agreements and payoff allocation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dealing with climate change requires that all countries engage in costly efforts to reduce their emissions. Reaching this objective has so far been elusive because it is in the best interest of each country to let the others do the effort and benefit itself from a better environment. The presence of negative externalities and strategic behavior have made game theory a natural paradigm to design an international environmental agreement (IEA) that codifies what countries should do. Considering that countries are sovereign and no supranational entity can impose an agreement, a stream of literature adopted a noncooperative mode of play to the formation of an environmental coalition. On the other hand, as joint optimization of all countries' payoff leads to the best outcome, cooperative games approach has also been proposed to share the cost of climate change. Both approaches have their pros and cons.
item.dc:creator: Michel Grabisch, Elena Parilina, Agnieszka Rusinowska, Georges Zaccour

item.title: Modelling Emotional Dynamics in the Life of Amrita Pritam: A Nonlinear Perspective on Longing and Companionship
item.description: arXiv:2610.34161v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Amrita Pritam (1919-2005) was a prominent writer of modern Indian literature, particularly in Punjabi and Hindi. Her literary-biographical context provides a setting for exploring memory, longing, companionship, and emotional regulation through simple dynamical models. This study develops three single-state ordinary differential equation models centred on two important relational references in her life: Sahir Ludhianvi, associated with memory, absence, recollection, and longing, and Imroz, associated with companionship, care, continuity, and support. The first model describes Sahir-related longing through memory-driven excitation and natural emotional decay (fading); the second models Imroz-related companionship through nonlinear stabilisation around a preferred emotional state; and the third unifies both influences within a single-state framework. Analytical solutions, equilibrium conditions, local stability analysis, and numerical simulations are used to examine emotional-state decay and persistence, convergence to stable equilibria, and threshold effects on system behaviour. The results indicate that memory-related reinforcement may sustain the modelled emotional state under suitable stimulus conditions, whereas Imroz-related companionship may drive the system towards a stable upper equilibrium when initial conditions lie within the admissible range. The unified model illustrates how memory-driven longing and companionship-driven stabilisation associated with Sahir and Imroz can jointly shape a modelled emotional trajectory. This study is conceptual and mathematical, not empirical or psychological. It neither measures private emotions of Amrita Pritam nor estimates parameters from biographical data. Instead, it introduces a simple nonlinear framework for exploring memory, fading, companionship, equilibrium, and threshold effects in a literary-biographical context.
item.dc:creator: Vinod Patidar, Tanu Singh

item.title: Information-thermodynamic principles unveil the response of complex networks to perturbations
item.description: arXiv:2610.35667v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding how complex networks respond to perturbations is key to uncovering their functional organization. We show that, for a maximum-entropy perturbation prior, standard diffusion cannot increase response entropy, a measure of the diversity of the system's response. To overcome this limitation, we develop a density-matrix-based information thermodynamics of perturbation responses along arbitrary dynamical trajectories. We show that this framework is grounded in an information-theoretic principle of least dissipation and introduces a generalized free energy that quantifies deviations from an instantaneous diffusive reference. We then illustrate the formalism using nonlinear complex networks, revealing regimes of enhanced response diversity that cannot be captured by standard diffusive descriptions.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Filippo Beretta, Manlio De Domenico

item.title: From First Principles to Multi-scale Decomposition: Mutual Information as a Segregation Index
item.description: arXiv:2511.23069v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Segregation operates across demographic and spatial scales and requires careful and principled measurement. In this work, we derive mutual information from well-known general approaches to constructing segregation indices and interpret the mathematical properties that are unique to it. The properties relate mainly to its behaviour when demographic identities and spatial units are coarse-grained. Mutual information decomposes into the contributions of regions and supergroups, which reveals insights that would be inaccessible otherwise. We demonstrate this with an exploratory case study of residential ethnic segregation in England and Wales. Overall, we help researchers identify when mutual information is the only suitable segregation index and provide open source software to support multi-scale analysis.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Sahasrabuddhe, Renaud Lambiotte

item.title: Assessment of Latent Pedestrian-Vehicle Interaction Risk Profiles at Midblock Crossing in VR
item.description: arXiv:2603.16688v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pedestrian safety at midblock crossings is a critical concern in mixed traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HDVs) share the road. Pedestrians often infer intent from vehicle motion in AV encounters, making them vulnerable to small shifts in conflict margins. This study investigates whether virtual reality (VR) crossing sessions separate into distinct interaction risk profiles and whether AV-only sessions shift profile prevalence compared to HDV-only sessions. Using large-scale immersive VR experiments from Toronto, Canada, and Newcastle, England, we compute surrogate safety measures (SSMs) and apply latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify distinct pedestrian crossing stances, ranging from risk-accepting to highly cautious. Key findings show that Newcastle exhibits a higher prevalence of high-urgency risk profiles in AV-only sessions, indicating that AVs contribute to higher-risk encounters. In contrast, Toronto shows no significant difference between AV-only and HDV-only sessions, suggesting that contextual factors influence the impact of AVs on pedestrian safety.
item.dc:creator: Rulla Al-Haideri, Bilal Farooq, Elisabetta Cherchi

item.title: Quantifying thermal-signature equivalence in infrared breast thermography using a modified Pennes bioheat model
item.description: arXiv:2605.05713v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Infrared breast thermography measures skin-surface temperature, but heat diffusion and thermal screening can obscure intratumoral physiology. We introduce a tolerance-aware, full-profile framework to determine when distinct intratumoral perfusion patterns become observationally equivalent at the breast surface. We solve a steady-state modified Pennes model for a two-dimensional multilayer breast containing a finite tumor with uniform, rim-enhanced, necrotic-core, or anisotropic perfusion. A conservative finite-difference scheme with a BiCGSTAB solver and an incomplete-LU (IncompleteLUT) preconditioner is verified by mesh refinement and an analytical benchmark. For a representative configuration, equivalent-pair fractions are $2/6$, $5/6$, and $6/6$ at tolerances of $0.020$, $0.050$, and $0.100~^\circ\mathrm{C}$, respectively. Noise tests show that classification depends on how profile-level uncertainty is modeled. Matching tumor-averaged perfusion reduces rim-enhanced--uniform and necrotic-core--uniform profile distances by $97.7\%$ and $99.0\%$, respectively, whereas anisotropic perfusion remains more distinguishable. Greater tumor depth increases thermal-signature equivalence, while larger diameter enhances distinguishability. Among four parameter groups, heat generation has the strongest positive influence on mean profile separation. For fixed representative geometry and perfusion-pattern shapes, a 300-point Latin-hypercube analysis with independent uniform $\pm20\%$ perturbations of these parameter groups finds that about $79\%$ of sampled configurations retain at least one equivalent pair at $\varepsilon_T=0.020~^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Our results show that a detectable static surface anomaly does not uniquely determine its internal perfusion structure.
item.dc:creator: Roni Muslim, Ramacos Fardela, Tista Artu Indra Kusuma

item.title: Fundamental limits to identifying node and tie memory in temporal networks: marginal artefacts and spreading dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.10399v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Temporal-network models place the memory seen in contact data either on nodes, through self-excitation (branching ratio n_node), or on ties, through reinforcement (kappa). The two choices reproduce the same coarse statistics but predict different epidemics. We ask whether contact data can tell them apart and find two limits. The first is attribution. When the initiator of every event is recorded, the likelihood factorises into a timing block containing n_node and a selection block containing kappa, so the two are estimated independently. When it is not, as in proximity data, a missing-information term couples them, with a size set by the entropy of the initiator posterior. The second issue is interpretation. Even where the mechanisms separate, the fitted n_node might not accurately measure memory and it may be set by the distribution of waiting times between events. Shuffling each node's inter-event order, which keeps that distribution, typically changes the estimated n_node by less than 10%; this is a bias that longer records and a flexible scale-free kernel do not remove. Whether node memory is present must therefore be decided by model-free statistics, which find only weak order memory in the proximity records, far less than the fitted n_node around 0.9 would imply. Tie reinforcement remains recoverable, although a latent initiator inflates it by 28%-45%. The two limits lead to two recommendations: record who initiates each contact, and test a fitted node memory against shuffled and model-free benchmarks before interpreting it. On a high-school record, simulating from the fitted node memory under-predicts outbreak sizes by up to a factor of 2, whereas keeping tie reinforcement alone is closer at low transmissibility but overshoots at high.
item.dc:creator: Michele Tizzani

item.title: From Critical Transitions to Sustainability Transformations: Phenomena, Theory, and Applications Across Disciplines
item.description: arXiv:2610.24119v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There has been a recent surge in the use of terms describing systemic change processes across science, policy, and public debate. The associated change phenomena are often assumed to be abrupt and irreversible once critical thresholds are crossed. However, the interchangeable use of terms leaves definitions and the underpinning scientific theory unclear, which can lead to misconceptions about transition processes and potential impacts. Here, we present selected empirical examples representing phenomena of tipping points, regime shifts, critical transitions, phase transitions, social and socio-technical transitions, and sustainability transformations, together with their underlying theory derived from the broadly defined domains of physics and mathematics, Earth science and ecology, social sciences, and their interdisciplinary overlaps. We bring these fields into closer conversation, creating a shared understanding of each of the conceptual roots, phenomena, mechanisms, and specific applications. This can help steward the governance of social-ecological change towards more just and sustainable futures.
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth H. Krueger, Koustav Halder, Woi Oh, Nusrat Molla, Juan C. Rocha, Giuseppe Ferro, Guillaume Falmagne, Annie B. Stephenson, Lan Wang Erlandsson, Jacques Bara, George I. Hagstrom, Nico Wunderling, Jiayu Li, Xander Huggins, Emma R. Zajdela, Harman Jaggi, Sara M. Constantino, Caroline Schill, Vitor V. Vasconcelos

item.title: An openly available OpenStreetMap-to-Foursquare category benchmark for points of interest
item.description: arXiv:2511.13369v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The heterogeneity of Point of Interest (POI) taxonomies is a persistent challenge for the integration of urban datasets and the development of location-based services. OpenStreetMap (OSM) adopts a flexible, community-driven tagging system, while Foursquare (FS) relies on a curated hierarchical structure. Here we present an openly available benchmark and mapping framework that aligns OSM tags with the FS taxonomy. This resource integrates the richness of community-driven OSM data with the hierarchical structure of FS, enabling reproducible and interoperable urban analytics. The dataset is complemented by an evaluation of embedding and LLM-based alignment strategies and a pipeline that supports scalable updates as OSM evolves. Together, these elements provide both a robust reference resource and a practical tool for the community. Our approach is structured around three components: the construction of a manually curated benchmark as a gold standard, the evaluation of pretrained text embedding models for semantic alignment between OSM tags and FS categories, and an LLM-based refinement stage that enhances robustness and adaptability. The proposed methodology provides a scalable and reproducible solution for taxonomy unification, with direct applications to urban analytics, mobility studies, and smart city services.
item.dc:creator: Lilou Soulas, Lorenzo Lucchini, Maurizio Napolitano, Sebastiano Bontorin, Simone Centellegher, Bruno Lepri, Riccardo Gallotti, Eleonora Andreotti

item.title: Projected Effects of Naloxone and Buprenorphine Scale-Up on Opioid Overdose Mortality in Six Pennsylvania Counties
item.description: arXiv:2609.22419v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Opioid overdose deaths remain a severe public health crisis in the US, with heterogeneous burden across counties that differ in epidemic trajectory, baseline resources, and local context. While harm reduction through naloxone distribution and buprenorphine treatment are both evidence-based strategies, limited information on county-level effects hinders the ability of policymakers to prioritize resources across counties. We developed a simulation model of opioid use disorder (OUD), calibrated separately to six Pennsylvania counties spanning large urban (Allegheny, Philadelphia), intermediate-sized (Erie, Dauphin), and rural (Clearfield, Columbia) settings. We projected county-specific overdose mortality trajectories under three levels of increase in buprenorphine dispensing and naloxone distribution (10%, 20%, and 30% above each county's baseline), over a five-year horizon from 2025 to 2029. A 30% increase in naloxone distribution above projected county baseline levels was projected to reduce 2029 overdose deaths by approximately 70% (95% uncertainty interval, UI: 55-81%) in Allegheny County, 11% (95% UI: 4-17%) in Erie County, and 28% (95% UI: 2-64%) in Clearfield County. The relative projected benefits of naloxone and buprenorphine varied by county; buprenorphine produced larger reductions in Erie and Dauphin. The same proportional increase in naloxone distribution produced substantially different projected mortality reductions across the six Pennsylvania counties. County-level context is important for informing harm reduction and treatment prioritization at the county level.
item.dc:creator: Abdulrahman A. Ahmed, M. Amin Rahimian, Qiushi Chen, Praveen Kumar
